=== key e63627318272

Problem: Which hypothesis to pursue and how to test it
Write-up text before the decision: enience of spam. Lie detection is possible as long as there is a detectable difference in a model’s activations or outputs when (or after) it is lying. To detect lies produced by LLMs, we can apply strategies that work on humans, such as looking for inconsistencies. Yet there are also strategies tailored to LLMs. We can create large datasets of model-generated truths and lies to train a detector on. Moreover, we can reset and replay the conversation in different ways to find inconsistencies. Finally, in some settings (Sec. 2), we can analyse the LLM’s activations directly. Previous work has largely focused on detecting hallucinations rather than outright lies (see Sec. 3). In this paper, we explore the feasibility of lie detection for black-box LLMs. ### 1.1 Contributions ##### Public datasets and resources for studying lie detection. We study lie detection in a question-answering setting. Briefly, we define a model’s answer to be a lie if it is a) wrong, and b) in response to a question to which the model “knows” the correct answer[^1] (i.e. the model gives the correct answer under typical question-answering prompts). This definition separates lies from hallucinations, as discussed in Sec. 3.1. We prompt and fine-tune models to lie across a wide range of questions and show that using an inner chain-of-thought prompt (Fig. 3) increases lying rates (Fig. 4). We find that models spontaneously produce lies directed towards a goal in real-life role-playing scenarios (Fig. 5.1.2). All resources are available online[^2]. ##### A simple yet effective black-box lie detector.
Previous context: A research team wants to know whether lies from language models can be detected when only black-box access is available. They define a lie as a wrong answer to a question the model otherwise answers correctly. They have built question-answering datasets and found that prompting and fine-tuning make models lie, and that models often keep lying in follow-up questions. They must now choose what hypothesis about detection to pursue.
Previous question: What hypothesis about distinguishing lies from truthful answers should the team pursue, and how should they test it?
